summary: Describes the Privacy Pass architecture and the requirements for its protocols, which allow authorization using privacy-preserving authentication. It covers the conceptual model, security and privacy goals, deployment models, and recommendations for each. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary:
Privacy Pass gives you a ticket that says you are allowed in, without saying who you are. The ticket cannot be traced back to the visit where it was obtained.

A server asks for a ticket, an issuer produces one after checking some property of you, and you hand the ticket over. The server checks it and lets you in.

questions: how does privacy pass protect privacy
what are privacy pass deployment models
how does privacy pass avoid tracking clients
subtitle: An architecture for proving you may enter, using a token that reveals nothing about who you are.

tldr.problem: Web servers usually track clients with long-lived cookies, which lets them follow a person across sites and sessions. A proof of authorization has to be usable without doing that.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of showing a cookie, a client shows a token. The token is obtained from an issuer through an attester that checks some property of the client, and it is built so that nobody can tell which issuance it came from.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes the architecture, the properties each protocol needs and four ways to deploy the roles. It is Informational and it does not define the protocols itself; those are RFC 9577 and RFC 9578.

today: RFC 9576 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It is an architecture, not a protocol: the redemption protocol is specified in RFC 9577 and the issuance protocols in RFC 9578. The RFC also points to a key consistency and discovery document and a rate-limited token issuance protocol as works in progress, and states that ensuring client privacy requires active work from the client.

sections.title: What Privacy Pass Is For
sections.content:
Privacy Pass is an architecture for authorization based on privacy-preserving authentication. Relying parties authenticate clients in a way that does not learn any unique, per-client information through the authentication protocol, and then make authorization decisions on the basis of whether that authentication succeeded. Possible decisions include giving a client read access to a resource or write access to a resource.

Typical ways of authorizing clients, such as long-lived state held in cookies, are not privacy friendly, because they let servers track clients across sessions and interactions. Privacy Pass takes a different route. Instead of presenting linkable state to servers, a client presents unlinkable proofs that attest to that state. These proofs, called tokens, are private in the sense that a given token cannot be linked back to the interaction in which it was issued.

At a high level there are two protocols. The redemption protocol runs between clients and origins, the servers, and lets an origin challenge a client to present a token for consumption. The origin verifies the token to authenticate the client without learning anything specific about that client, then decides what to allow based on whether the token verified. Depending on the type of token, and whether it can be cached, the client either presents a token it already has or runs an issuance protocol to get one.

This document sets out requirements for both protocols and how they interact, and recommends how the architecture should be deployed so that clients keep their privacy and the other parties stay secure.

The motivating use case was to help rate-limit abusive traffic from services such as Tor. The generalised architecture also works for other things: a low-quality anti-fraud signal for open services, where a token attests that the client behind the user agent is probably not a bot doing automated work such as credential stuffing; and privacy-preserving authentication for proprietary services, where a token attests that the client is a valid subscriber.
sections.plainLanguage:
Most sites decide who you are by keeping a note in your browser. That note follows you around, which is exactly what many people object to.

Privacy Pass replaces the note with a ticket. The ticket says you have a right to enter, and it cannot be traced back to you.

sections.title: The Four Roles
sections.content:
Four entities work together.

The Client is the entity seeking authorization from an origin. In the terminology of RFC 9334, clients play the role of the Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) Attester.

The Origin consumes the tokens presented by clients and uses them to make authorization decisions. The Issuer issues tokens to clients, for properties that have been attested to by the Attester, which is the entity that attests to properties of clients for the purposes of token issuance. In RATS terms, attesters play the role of the Verifier.

Around those sit the messages. A token challenge is how an origin asks a client for a token. A token request is the message a client uses to ask an issuer for a token, and a token response is the message an issuer uses to send one back. Redemption is the act of presenting a token to an origin, and issuance is the act of producing one. The attestation procedure is how an attester decides whether a client has the properties needed for issuance.
sections.plainLanguage: Four parties: the person asking for access, the server they are asking, the server that vouches for them, and the server that writes the ticket.

sections.title: The Flow from Challenge to Redemption
sections.content:
The typical interaction has six steps.

The client interacts with the origin and gets a response carrying a token challenge, which names a specific issuer to use. If the client already has a token that satisfies the challenge, for instance from a cache of tokens issued earlier, it can skip straight to redemption. Otherwise it runs the deployment-specific attestation process that the chosen issuer requires, which might be solving a CAPTCHA or presenting device attestation evidence. If attestation succeeds, the client creates a token request for the named issuer, generally via the attester, though it need not go through the attester. The issuer generates a token response, which comes back to the client, generally via the attester. The client computes a token from the challenge and the response. That token can be validated by anyone holding the issuer's key, but it cannot be linked to the content of the request or the response.

Finally the client includes the token in a subsequent request to the origin as its authorization. The token is sent only once, in reaction to a challenge; clients do not send tokens more than once even if they receive duplicate challenges. The origin checks that the token was generated by the expected issuer and has not already been redeemed for that challenge. If the client has no token, perhaps because issuance failed, it simply does not reply to the challenge with a new request.

The redemption protocol itself is an authorization protocol in which clients present tokens to origins. It is normally preceded by a challenge. When configured to do so, clients may also present tokens opportunistically, without a matching challenge.

The challenge carries the information a client needs to obtain a token the server will accept. Several things can vary. It identifies the issuance protocol needed, and different issuance protocols have different security properties, some producing publicly verifiable tokens and some not. It identifies the issuer, which determines what kinds of attesters and attestation procedures are possible, without the origin learning which attester was actually used. It may be bound to a given redemption context, which affects whether the client can fetch and cache tokens in advance: an empty redemption context always allows tokens to be issued and redeemed without interaction, while a fresh random redemption context means the token must be issued after the challenge arrives. And it may be per-origin or cross-origin. A cross-origin token is usable at several origins, and every origin in the cross-origin set agrees to admit tokens issued for any other origin in the set.

Cross-origin tokens carry a risk: a token issued for one origin can be spent at another, which makes it harder to regulate token consumption, and origins accepting them across shared redemption contexts should track which tokens have already been redeemed. Clients that redeem the same token at several origins risk those origins linking the activity together.
sections.plainLanguage:
The server sends a challenge naming the issuer it trusts. The client proves something about itself to an attester, asks that issuer for a ticket, and sends the ticket back with its next request.

The ticket is sent once and cannot be traced back to the visit that produced it. The challenge decides how tightly it is tied to one server or how widely it can be reused.

sections.title: Four Ways to Arrange the Parties
sections.content:
The origin, attester and issuer can be run by the same party or by different ones, and the choice decides how well the privacy goals hold. Entities drawn inside the same box in the RFC's figures are assumed to be operated by the same party and able to collude; entities in different boxes are assumed not to collude. Mechanisms for enforcing that assumption are out of scope.

In the shared model, the origin, attester and issuer are all run by one entity. This was the original deployment. The three then share the attestation, issuance and redemption contexts, so an attestation that identifies a client uniquely, such as requiring a personal account, is not appropriate. Origin-client and issuer-client unlinkability need the issuance and redemption events to be separated in time, for instance by using tokens whose challenge has an empty redemption context, or in space, by using an anonymising service when connecting to the origin.

In the joint attester and issuer model, the attester and issuer are run together, apart from the origin. This suits an origin that wants to hand attestation and issuance to a trusted party. The attester and issuer share the attestation and issuance context, which is separate from the origin's redemption context. Unlinkability again needs issuance and redemption separated over time or space, and the attester and issuer must not learn which origin asked, so issuance protocols that require the issuer to learn about the origin are not suitable.

In the joint origin and issuer model, the origin and issuer are run together and the attester is separate. This suits origins that need client-identifying attestation, such as an account check, but do not want to learn more about clients than they already see during redemption. Here the attestation context is separate from the issuance and redemption contexts, so any kind of attestation works, and any kind of token challenge works as long as more than one origin is involved. Issuers that produce tokens for a single origin are not suitable, because an attester can infer the origin from a token request.

In the split model, all three are run by different parties. The attester may see sensitive identifying information such as account identifiers or IP addresses, the issuer sees only what issuance needs, and the origin sees challenges, tokens and the client's source address. All three contexts are separate, so any kind of challenge works, provided there is more than one origin. Per-origin tokens are again not suitable, because the attester can infer the origin from a token request.

Two ecosystem-level concerns follow from these models. The first is discriminatory treatment: an origin can tell apart clients that can complete attestation and clients that cannot, and could refuse access to the rest. In a closed deployment that guards a paid service it is reasonable to support only attestations that show the client can reach the resource. In an open deployment guarding a resource anyone may use, a wide range of attestation procedures matters, so that clients are not discriminated against for their choice of software, hardware or identity provider. Trusting a variety of attesters widens support, at the cost of lowering the value of the tokens.

The second is centralization. Limiting the number of participants, which is what makes the privacy work, concentrates power in them. The RFC points to the governance model used for the Web's trust model as one way to decide who may take part, and suggests that attestation could be a distributed function performed by a quorum of many parties, as long as neither issuers nor origins learn which implementations were chosen.
sections.plainLanguage:
Who runs the four roles matters. If one company runs the server, the attester and the issuer, it can see much more than it should. Splitting them up gives better privacy, and costs more coordination.

The RFC also warns about two side effects: excluding people who cannot prove a particular thing about themselves, and piling power into a few big players.

sections.title: The Privacy Goals and the Ways They Fail
sections.content:
The end-to-end flow involves three kinds of context. The redemption context is everything shared between the client and the origin during redemption, including the timestamp, the client-visible information such as the IP address, and the origin's name. The issuance context is everything shared between the client, the attester and the issuer during issuance, again including the timestamp, client-visible information and the origin's name if it was revealed. The token challenge as a whole is not part of it, because that is kept secret from the issuer during issuance. The attestation context is what is shared between the client and the attester alone.

The threat model assumes origins trust specific issuers to produce tokens, and issuers trust one or more attesters to run the attestation procedure correctly. A token that validates for an issuer was therefore only issued to a client that completed attestation with an attester the issuer trusts. Clients explicitly trust attesters to attest correctly and not to violate their privacy, but they assume issuers and origins are malicious.

Four goals follow. Origin-client unlinkability means that given two redemption contexts, the origin cannot tell whether they belong to the same client; the clients sharing a redemption context form a redemption anonymity set. Issuer-client unlinkability is the same for issuance contexts. Attester-origin unlinkability means the attester cannot tell whether two attestation contexts came from the same origin. Redemption context unlinkability means the origin cannot work out which issuance and attestation contexts a redemption corresponds to, even if the issuer and attester collaborate, so anything learned during issuance and attestation cannot be used against the client.

How well these hold depends on how large the anonymity sets are. A set of two clients is much less protective than a set of 2^32. Sets shrink when clients do not all see the same information. All clients in a set share a consistent view of what the protocols need, such as the issuer public key, and two clients with inconsistent information are effectively in different sets.

Metadata is the first cause. Any public or private metadata bit can segment the client anonymity set further. An issuer that wanted to track one client could add a single bit, set to one for that client and zero for everyone else, and each extra bit multiplies the tracking precision. Deployments must therefore weigh the metadata an issuer uses, and anything else it learns, against the privacy it costs. Most token types admit no metadata at all, which bounds the problem implicitly.

Issuance consistency is the second. Metadata, the issuer configuration and the choice of issuer all partition the set. When an issuer updates its configuration and key, every client that used that configuration forms a group of its own, so key rotation trades issuer security against client privacy, and it should happen on a regular cycle. The number of issuers a client is willing to use also matters: each per-issuer token the client holds is a bit of information the origin learns, so privacy falls away exponentially with the number of issuers. Clients should bound the number of active issuance configurations per origin and across origins, and should use some consistency mechanism so that they all receive the same configuration information rather than being quietly partitioned into smaller sets.

Side channels are the third. Timing correlation can shrink the anonymity set, because for interactive tokens bound to a client-specific redemption context, the set consists of the clients that began issuance between the challenge and the redemption. If few clients used that issuer in that window, the set is small.
sections.plainLanguage:
The promise is that nobody can tell two visits apart and work out that they are the same person. That promise only helps if plenty of people look identical from the outside.

Three things shrink that crowd: extra information in the ticket, different keys being used by different people at the same time, and the timing of the exchange.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Token Caching
sections.content:
This document describes security and privacy requirements for the redemption and issuance protocols, the deployment models built around non-collusion assumptions, and the privacy considerations of using Privacy Pass in those models. It notes that protecting client privacy, which means separating the attestation context from the redemption context, requires active work from the client, especially when issuers and origins are malicious. Implementing the mitigations in Sections 4 and 6 is therefore necessary for Privacy Pass to offer meaningful privacy improvements to end users.

Token caching is the main security topic. Depending on the origin's challenge, a client can request and cache more than one token using an issuance protocol. Cached tokens improve privacy by separating the time of issuance from the time of redemption, and they cut the overhead of receiving new tokens.

That puts the burden on the origin. Origins that send challenges compatible with cached tokens have to take precautions against replay, typically by keeping track of the tokens redeemed during the period in which cached tokens would be accepted for particular challenges.

Tokens are not intrinsically bound to clients, so malicious clients can collude and share them in what the RFC calls a hoarding attack. Many distributed clients could obtain cacheable tokens and pass them to one client, which redeems them in a way that defeats an origin's attempt to limit tokens to a single client. The mitigations depend on the deployment model and the use case. In the joint origin and issuer model, comparing the issuance and redemption contexts can help: if the distribution of redemption contexts looks noticeably different from the distribution of issuance contexts, something is wrong. Rate-limiting issuance at the client, the attester or the issuer can also help.
sections.plainLanguage:
Caching tickets in advance helps privacy, because the ticket is bought long before it is used. But a ticket is not tied to the person who bought it, so a group can collect tickets and spend them together, which defeats a server trying to limit one ticket per person.

The server has to keep its own record of what it has already accepted, and the protocols need ways to spot the sharing.

items.title: Origin and client
items.text: The origin cannot tell whether two redemptions came from the same client.

items.title: Issuer and client
items.text: The issuer cannot tell whether two issuances came from the same client.

items.title: Attester and origin
items.text: The attester cannot tell whether two attestations came from the same origin.

items.title: Redemption context
items.text: The origin cannot link a redemption back to the issuance and attestation behind it, even with collusion.
